messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mere, a 66-year-old divorced shopowner of Oceania background, described the event that had split her life into before and after: one evening, at nearly the same hour she now finds unbearable, police officers came to her business and forced her to the ground in a confrontation she still struggled to assemble fully. She could remember the harsh light, the sense of being watched by uniforms closing in on her, and the sickening dizziness that hit her as she was pinned and told to stay still. What remained were jagged fragments rather than a complete account. There were stretches she could not recover no matter how hard she tried, and the extremity of it left her with the feeling that it could hardly have happened to her at all. When she attempted to speak about it, the words seemed to stop at the edge of her throat; the memory felt too stark, too bodily, too humiliating to translate into a story. In the months that followed, Mere began to interpret her reactions as proof that something was wrong with her. She was convinced that reacting this way meant she was inadequate, a lousy coper, and at times she feared that the way her mind lurched and blanked under stress meant she was going crazy.

Certain moments now pulled her straight back toward that night. If the day moved into the same time of evening when the police had arrived, her chest tightened and she would feel the first hint of dizziness again; if she sensed someone lingering nearby as if observing her, the old alarm surged. Those moments did not stay abstract. They pushed her into action almost immediately, because being in the dark, or in any circumstance that reminded her of the event, became intolerable. She began avoiding the shop after dusk and made excuses not to attend evening family gatherings, especially around dates and anniversaries connected to the incident. The more she reshaped her life around these fears, the more she found herself returning to the memory in pieces. In the quiet of the shop after closing, or when she caught a passing glimpse of the street at that same hour, the scene came back with the gaps still there, and she was left trying to make sense of a story she could not properly tell. That unfinished quality made the whole event feel even more unreal to her, and the more unreal it felt, the more she doubted herself.

Mere’s efforts to blunt the distress had their own cost. She had started spending money impulsively, buying unnecessary stock and small comforts for the shop or home in the moment, telling herself she was simply trying to distract herself or feel calmer. For a little while this gave her something else to focus on, but afterward she was left with the same gaps and the same dread, and sometimes even more uneasy because she recognized how unplanned her choices had been. She thought this was further evidence that she was not coping properly, and the shame of that belief fed back into her fear that she was inadequate. The spending also brought back the very sensations she was trying to avoid: the stress of sorting bills, the late-night calculations, the sense of being trapped under pressure, all of which could make her feel watched and unsettled again, as though the old police presence had seeped into ordinary life. On evenings when she was alone in the shop, the memory and the present seemed to blur together; the more she tried to push the memory away, the less available it became in any orderly form, and the more it returned as dizziness, dread, and self-criticism.

Over time, Mere’s world narrowed. She stayed away from the dark, avoided commemorative dates, and arranged her workday so she would not be alone at the worst hour, though this was difficult to sustain in a small business. Her daughter had noticed that she was no longer the steady shopowner she used to be. What finally brought Mere to seek help was a recent evening shift when a customer stood outside the doorway watching for a long moment, and the familiar wave of lightheadedness hit so sharply that she had to grip the counter to steady herself. She closed early, went home frightened by how quickly the old scene had flooded back, and sat awake worrying that she could not keep living around these moments forever. She came to therapy hoping to understand why her mind kept breaking the memory into pieces and why she felt so ashamed of herself, but she was most afraid that the feeling of being watched, the dizzy rush, and the sense that she was losing control would continue to spread through her life until there was nowhere left that felt safe.
